scenes.narration: Nobody designed the part of Demon (comics) you experience — it was inherited. The comic, which follows a man who apparently cannot die, was self-published from 2014 to 2016 as a mini-comic and webcomic, then released as a four-volume, 720-page graphic novel by First Second Books in 2016 and 2017. It was unusually well-organized for a webcomic, having been entirely written and laid out before its release, with a well-founded story, consistent art, and daily updates.

Every serious account of Demon (comics) eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. The comic was received favourably by critics, who praised the clever story; its puzzles and plot twists; the artwork, which balanced the often grim subject matter; and the surprising humor. Jimmy concludes that he is a "demon", and that each time he dies, his mind possesses the closest person.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Demon (comics) — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Jimmy attempts to provoke a suicide by cop, attacking Hunter, but is overpowered. Hunter locks the fatally injured Jimmy in a supermax prison death row cell so that Jimmy will possess the neighbouring inmate.

The selfish-gene reading of Demon (comics) makes it less romantic and far more precise. Jimmy improvises a weapon and suicides through dozens of condemned prisoners until he possesses a guard and escapes. Jimmy plans to kill an imprisoned drunk driver to avenge his family.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. The OSS set a trap, but both parties are surprised to find that Jimmy's 10-year-old daughter, Sweet Pea, is a demon possessing the brain-damaged drunk driver. Hunter attempts another trap, but Jimmy kills the entire group and reunites with Sweet Pea.

The feeling that Demon (comics) means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. It is explained that the OSS had planned to make demons to replace hostile dictators with US puppets. Jimmy is offered a pardon to kill Gellman, who they say plans to attack the US.

Nothing in Demon (comics) was built for you — it was built for reproduction. Jimmy agrees, but goes rogue and provokes a military response to destroy the OSS base. Jimmy decides that he and Sweet Pea should quietly outlive any remaining adversaries.

The psychology underneath Demon (comics) is simpler and older than the story on top. When they meet, Gellman kills himself, ending his long life; the next-closest person is Jimmy, another demon, who cannot be possessed. Jimmy is bored with life, feeling that the best is behind him.

Behind Demon (comics) sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. Jimmy unexpectedly walks into a trap set by Hunter, who had demonized himself before the lab was destroyed. Following an extended fight and chase, during which Jimmy phones Sweet Pea to warn her, Hunter executes Jimmy.

The nihilist does not deny Demon (comics) — he only refuses to flatter it. The OSS find Sweet Pea and imprison her at Osaka Castle, but she is able to send secret messages. Hunter plans to harvest Sweet Pea's blood over several months to make a demon army and replace world leaders.

What culture calls destiny in Demon (comics) is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Six months later, he executes her and harvests her remaining blood to complete his army. Later, Jimmy is born, possesses an adult, and sends a message to Sweet Pea.

The genes do not care about Demon (comics); they care about copies. Seven months earlier, Sweet Pea receives Jimmy's warning that Hunter is still alive. She faces a dilemma: the only way to locate Hunter is to be captured, but if she is captured, she will not be able to fight Hunter.

Take away the meaning and Demon (comics) still functions — that is the disturbing part. She recalls that each possession creates a parallel universe in which the possessor survives the suicide attempt. Sweet Pea possesses an astronaut and suicides in outer space, where the next-closest human is the same astronaut in a parallel universe.

The unconscious does not argue with Demon (comics); it simply acts first. One of them is captured, and the other receives the prisoner's messages and plans an attack. Months later, the free Sweet Pea receives Jimmy's message and they reunite.

Demon (comics) feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Sweet Pea declares victory, but they both find life boring and decide to stop Hunter. They spend a month training, then create hundreds of duplicates using the entire human population in space.

The bleak reading of Demon (comics) is also the most testable one. Hours before Hunter's scheduled world takeover, they launch their attack, with high casualties on both sides. The castle gate becomes a killing zone, and Hunter releases failsafes, killing friend and foe.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Demon (comics). Jimmy directly engages and overpowers Hunter, who orders the lab guards to reinforce him. Hunter wants Jimmy to witness his victory, but Sweet Pea has taken over the lab – their actual goal – and exsanguinated one hundred duplicates to demonize every human on Earth.

The self that experiences Demon (comics) is a committee, not a king. Hunter's agents kill themselves in the planned coup, but there is no one left to possess. Far away from the battle, a Jimmy and a Sweet Pea watch news reports of the events.

Reproduction explains more of Demon (comics) than any philosophy dares to admit. With everyone a demon and no one to possess, they are all equal and mortal. Jimmy recalls that Gellman had said there was another way to make a possession, and considers the challenge of becoming a good person.

Once you see Demon (comics) as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Cartoonist Jason Shiga began working on Demon in 2010 when he had finished his previous title, Empire State. His earlier attempts at creating an epic work had both failed, and Shiga stated that his biggest obstacle to creating Demon was "figuring out how to do it" (emphasis in original).

The story Demon (comics) tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. He usually spends as much time planning a book as he does drawing it, and it took him about three years to write and pencil 720 pages for Demon. In order to construct the puzzles and mathematics in his stories, Shiga wrote from the ending and worked backwards.

Meaning is not found in Demon (comics) — it is manufactured for it. Shiga cut some story arcs while thumbnailing, and rewrote the last chapter twice. Shiga stated that the biggest influences on Demon were the Quantum Leap television series and the films Groundhog Day and Memoirs of an Invisible Man.

The cold light on Demon (comics) leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. Quantum Leap was his favourite show and inspired the possessions in the series, although he disliked that the leaps required performing good deeds. He was similarly disappointed with how good deeds broke the loop in Groundhog Day, feeling that there was no logic to it.

Demon (comics) did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. Shiga was also inspired by MacGyver, whose title character used intelligence to overcome obstacles with minimal resources, and by Death Note, in which two brilliant minds compete for advantage. The improvised weapon used to escape the prison was based on a real incident in Japan.

The honest version of Demon (comics) starts by giving up the comforting part. The final showdown at Osaka Castle was inspired by Shiga's visit there on his honeymoon. He was particularly influenced by an artist's interpretation of the Siege of Osaka in isometric perspective.

Strip Demon (comics) of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Shiga placed great importance on negative space in the layouts to control the pacing. The final art was inked in sequence, with coloring done in Photoshop.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Demon (comics) shows exactly where that breaks. Although many reviewers have noted that Shiga's simple artistic style contrasts with the wild plots, making them more palatable, Shiga has stated that he did not consciously do this and is critical of his artistic skill, feeling that it is a professional shortcoming. In 2013, Shiga submitted Demon to Abrams Books, which was publishing his previous title Empire State.

What looks like free choice in Demon (comics) is older than choice itself. Shiga was intransigent about the format and subject matter, and so decided to self-publish. Being solely responsible for production encouraged Shiga to "try every crazy idea I could get away with" – including issues of 4 pages, 60 pages, and one in which every panel was black.

Nobody designed the part of Demon (comics) you experience — it was inherited. Shiga initially released Demon as a mini-comic, which was a familiar format for him. He printed 400 copies of each issue on a Risograph printer, and mailed them out, believing that this would be the work's final form.

Every serious account of Demon (comics) eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Shiga had been skeptical about webcomics; as an afterthought he put some pages on his website in January 2014, where it gathered a larger following. Having the story entirely mapped out made Demon unusually organized for a webcomic, allowing him to publish seven pages per week and to also display a completion bar indicating the comic's progress toward its conclusion.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Demon (comics) — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Shiga improvised a little while inking the mini-comic and webcomic, adding to some arcs and cutting others. This resulted in an additional 15 pages compared to his penciled manuscript.

The selfish-gene reading of Demon (comics) makes it less romantic and far more precise. He became an early adopter of Patreon and was receiving $2,000 per month by the completion of the webcomic on 23 May 2016. The earnings and readership convinced publishers that Demon was a marketable title.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. The 21-issue comic was repackaged as a four-part graphic novel (released in four-month intervals during 2016 and 2017) with only small changes to the original material. Shiga stated that it split easily into four volumes, though he had wanted a single 720-page edition.
